lessons.title: Torque Check of Critical Fasteners
lessons.body: After assembling an EV motorbike, you must check the tightness of every critical bolt and nut. Loose fasteners can cause accidents. Use a calibrated torque wrench. For this module, you need a torque wrench that reads from 5 Nm to 100 Nm. Start with the front and rear axle nuts. The front axle nut should be tightened to 60 Nm. The rear axle nut to 80 Nm. Check the brake caliper bolts: front caliper bolts to 25 Nm, rear caliper bolts to 25 Nm. The handlebar clamp bolts to 20 Nm. The battery mounting bolts to 15 Nm. The motor mount bolts to 40 Nm. Always tighten in a star pattern if there are multiple bolts, like on the wheel. Use a torque wrench, not a regular spanner. If you don't have a torque wrench, borrow one from a nearby garage. In Africa, many workshops have torque wrenches for petrol bikes; they work the same. After tightening, mark each bolt with a paint pen so you know it's been checked. Do a final check after the first 50 km of riding, as some bolts may settle. Never overtighten, as you can strip threads or break the bolt. If you feel the wrench click, stop. If a bolt is stripped, replace it with a high-tensile steel bolt of the same size. Record all torque values in a logbook. This is your proof of quality. A well-torqued bike is a safe bike.

lessons.title: Fluid and Lubricant Top-Off
lessons.body: EV motorbikes have fewer fluids than petrol bikes, but you still need to check and top off several. First, brake fluid. Most EV bikes use DOT 3 or DOT 4 brake fluid. Check the reservoir on the handlebar and near the rear brake. The fluid should be between the MIN and MAX lines. If low, top up with fresh fluid from a sealed bottle. Never mix DOT 3 and DOT 4. Use a clean cloth to wipe any spills, as brake fluid damages paint. Second, battery coolant. Some high-performance EV bikes have liquid-cooled batteries and motors. Check the coolant level in the overflow tank. Use a 50/50 mix of distilled water and ethylene glycol coolant. If you live in a very hot area, use a 60/40 mix. Do not use tap water; it causes corrosion. Third, chain lubricant. If your bike has a chain drive, clean the chain with a brush and kerosene, then apply chain lube. Spin the wheel and spray the inside of the chain. Let it dry for 10 minutes. Fourth, check the gear oil in the reduction gearbox. Some EVs have a small gearbox that needs 80W-90 gear oil. Check the level with the dipstick or fill plug. Top off if needed. Fifth, check the brake pads and discs for wear. Replace pads if less than 2 mm thick. Finally, check tire pressure. Front tire: 28 psi, rear tire: 32 psi. Adjust for load. In Africa, roads can be rough, so slightly lower pressure improves grip. Always use a pressure gauge, not your thumb. Record all top-offs in your logbook.

lessons.title: Software Update and Calibration
lessons.body: Modern EV motorbikes have a controller, battery management system (BMS), and sometimes a display. These need software updates and calibration. First, connect your laptop or smartphone to the bike's diagnostic port. This is usually a USB or CAN bus connector under the seat. Use the manufacturer's app or software. If you don't have it, download it from the manufacturer's website. For many African brands, the software is free. Update the firmware to the latest version. This fixes bugs and improves performance. After updating, calibrate the throttle. Turn the key on, but don't twist the throttle. The system will learn the zero position. Then twist the throttle fully and hold for 3 seconds. Release. The system learns the full position. Next, calibrate the battery. Fully charge the battery, then ride until it is 20% remaining. Then fully charge again. This helps the BMS learn the true capacity. Also calibrate the speedometer. Use a GPS app on your phone to check actual speed. If the speedometer reads 40 km/h but GPS says 45 km/h, adjust the wheel size setting in the software. Finally, check for error codes. The display may show a wrench icon. Use the software to read and clear codes. If a code persists, check the sensor or wiring. Common codes: P0A0F (motor overheat), P0B0F (battery undervoltage). Fix issues before handover. Document the software version and calibration date in the logbook.

lessons.title: Cleaning and Detailing
lessons.body: A clean bike shows quality and makes the customer happy. Start by washing the bike. Use a bucket of water and a mild car shampoo. Do not use a high-pressure hose, as water can get into the battery, controller, and motor. Use a soft sponge or cloth. Wash from top to bottom. Rinse with a gentle stream of water. Dry with a microfiber cloth. Next, clean the battery pack and motor with a damp cloth only. Never spray water directly on electrical components. For the chain, use a degreaser and a brush, then rinse and dry, then apply chain lube. For the brakes, clean the calipers with brake cleaner and a toothbrush. Do not get brake cleaner on painted surfaces. For the body panels, use a plastic polish to restore shine. For the seat, use a vinyl cleaner. For the tires, use a tire shine, but avoid the tread. After cleaning, inspect for any damage: cracks, loose bolts, frayed cables. Touch up paint chips with matching paint. Replace any missing decals. Finally, polish the metal parts with chrome polish. In Africa, dust is a problem, so use a dust cover when parked. A clean bike also helps you spot leaks or cracks. Take pride in your work. A detailed bike sells itself. Handover a bike that looks new.

lessons.title: Documentation and Warranty Registration
lessons.body: Every EV motorbike you assemble must have proper paperwork. Start with the assembly checklist. This is a form that lists every step you did: torque checks, fluid top-offs, software updates, cleaning. Sign and date it. Next, fill out the warranty card. The customer gets one copy, you keep one. The warranty covers the battery for 2 years or 20,000 km, whichever comes first. The motor and controller for 1 year. The frame for 3 years. Write the serial number of the bike, the battery, and the motor. These are usually on a sticker or engraved. Take photos of the serial numbers. Next, create an invoice or receipt. Include the date, customer name, phone number, address, bike model, color, and price. If the customer paid a deposit, note the balance. Also, give the customer the owner's manual. If you don't have a printed manual, download a PDF and put it on a USB stick or send via WhatsApp. Next, register the bike with the local authorities if required. In many African countries, you need a license plate and insurance. Help the customer with this. Finally, keep a copy of all documents in a file. This protects you if there is a dispute. Also, record the customer's details in a database for future service reminders. Send a reminder after 500 km for the first service. Good documentation builds trust and repeat business.

lessons.title: Customer Handover and Basic Training
lessons.body: The handover is your chance to teach the customer how to use and care for their new EV motorbike. Start by showing them the controls: key ignition, throttle, brakes, lights, horn, and turn signals. Show them how to turn it on and off. Explain the battery gauge: green means full, yellow means half, red means charge soon. Show them how to charge: plug into a standard 220V socket, using the charger provided. Charge for 6-8 hours for a full charge. Do not leave it plugged in for more than 24 hours. Show them how to check tire pressure and brake fluid. Teach them the daily checks: tires, brakes, lights, battery level. Show them how to adjust the mirrors and handlebar. Explain the regenerative braking: when you release the throttle, the motor slows the bike and charges the battery. This saves energy. Warn them not to touch the battery terminals or open the battery box. If they have a problem, they should call you, not try to fix it themselves. Give them your phone number and the workshop address. Do a test ride with them: you ride first, then they ride in a safe area. Watch them start, stop, and turn. Correct any mistakes. Finally, give them the keys, documents, and a small toolkit. Wish them safe riding. A good handover creates a happy customer who will recommend you to others.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Final Inspection and Handover â Practical Reference

Final inspection is where an assembled electric motorbike stops being a pile of parts and becomes a saleable asset. In the African e-mobility market â Nairobi boda boda riders, Kigali delivery fleets, Kampala commercial riders, Lagos last-mile operators â the handover moment determines whether you get repeat business, warranty claims, or a damaged brand. This lesson gives you the shop-floor sequence, torque values, fluid specs, software steps, and the paperwork that protects both the customer and your margin. Treat it as your pre-delivery inspection (PDI) playbook.

Business reality: a single missed fastener or uncalibrated controller can cost you a full warranty replacement, a stranded rider, and lost fleet contracts worth tens of thousands of dollars. Every step below exists because someone, somewhere, paid for skipping it.

1. Torque Check of Critical Fasteners

Torque is not "tight enough." It is a measured value. On an e-motorbike the critical joints are: axle nuts, brake caliper bolts, steering stem nut, motor mount bolts, battery pack mounting bolts, and handlebar clamp bolts. Under-torque causes vibration loosening and catastrophic failure; over-torque strips threads, cracks castings, and deforms brake discs.

Use a calibrated torque wrench â never a rattle gun on critical joints. Record every value on the PDI sheet. In dusty African conditions, apply thread-locker (medium strength, e.g., Loctite 243) on motor mounts and caliper bolts, and re-check after the first 100 km.

Table 1 â Recommended torque values for critical e-motorbike fasteners (typical 1â3 kW hub-motor class)
Fastener / JointThreadTorque (NÂ·m)Notes
Rear axle nutM1480â100Re-check after 100 km
Front axle nutM1250â65Use thread-locker
Brake caliper boltsM822â28Critical safety item
Motor mount boltsM1035â45Medium thread-locker
Battery pack mounting boltsM818â24Do not over-compress
Steering stem nutM2260â80Check bearing play
Handlebar clamp boltsM820â25Tighten evenly, cross pattern

Source: Consolidated from manufacturer service manuals for hub-motor e-motorbikes (e.g., Ampersand, Roam, Spiro assembly guidelines) and general motorcycle torque standards. Always defer to your specific OEM manual â values vary by model.

2. Fluid and Lubricant Top-Off

Electric motorbikes have fewer fluids than ICE bikes, but the ones they have matter. Check and top off: brake fluid (DOT 3 or DOT 4, never mix), hydraulic brake lines for leaks, wheel bearing grease, suspension fork oil (if applicable), chain lubricant (on chain-drive models), and gearbox oil in hub or mid-drive motors that require it.

In hot, dusty African operating conditions, brake fluid absorbs moisture faster. Test with a brake fluid tester; replace if water content exceeds 3%. Use only sealed, fresh containers â opened fluid in a dusty workshop is contaminated fluid.

Table 2 â Fluid and lubricant specifications and service intervals
Fluid / LubricantSpecificationCheck IntervalReplace Interval
Brake fluidDOT 3 / DOT 4Every serviceEvery 12 months or if >3% water
Chain lubricantO-ring safe, dry or wax-basedEvery 300 kmClean & re-lube every 600 km
Wheel bearing greaseLithium complex NLGI 2Every 5,000 kmEvery 10,000 km
Fork oil (if applicable)OEM-specified weightEvery 10,000 kmEvery 20,000 km
Hub motor gear oil (if applicable)OEM-specified gear oilEvery 3,000 kmEvery 6,000 km

Source: Adapted from manufacturer service schedules and the U.S. Department of Energy Electric Vehicle Maintenance guidance, plus general motorcycle maintenance standards. Confirm against your OEM manual.

â  SAFETY WARNING â BRAKE FLUID & BATTERY HANDLING

Brake fluid is toxic, corrosive to paint, and absorbs moisture from the air. Do not open the reservoir in a dusty environment without cleaning the cap first. Never mix DOT 3 and DOT 4 unless the OEM explicitly allows it. For high-voltage battery packs (48Vâ72V), always disconnect the main fuse and wear insulated gloves before touching terminals. A shorted pack can cause arc flash, fire, or fatal shock. In African workshops with unreliable grounding, verify your earth connection before any electrical work.

3. Software Update and Calibration

Modern e-motorbikes have a controller (BLDC or FOC), a BMS, and often a display/telematics unit. Before handover you must: (1) check the controller firmware version against the latest OEM release; (2) update via the manufacturer's app or cable; (3) calibrate the throttle (zero and full position); (4) calibrate the brake cut-off switch; (5) verify speedometer accuracy against GPS; (6) check BMS cell balance and state of health (SoH).

Calibration matters commercially: a mis-calibrated throttle causes jerky acceleration, which riders interpret as a defective bike. A mis-reading speedometer creates legal and trust problems. Log the firmware version and calibration values on the PDI sheet â this is your evidence if a warranty dispute arises.

4. Cleaning and Detailing

A clean bike sells. But cleaning is also inspection: dirt hides cracks, leaks, and loose fasteners. Use low-pressure water only â never a pressure washer near the controller, motor connectors, display, or battery compartment. Use a soft brush and pH-neutral cleaner. Dry with compressed air or microfiber. Apply a protective spray to the frame and a silicone dressing to rubber parts.

In dusty African conditions, pay special attention to the air intake of the controller cooling system, the motor cooling fins, and the brake caliper area. Clogged cooling fins cause controller overheating â a leading cause of warranty returns in hot climates.

5. Documentation and Warranty Registration

This is where most African assemblers lose money. Incomplete paperwork means denied warranty claims. You need: a completed PDI checklist (signed), a warranty registration card with frame number (VIN), motor number, battery serial number, controller serial number, customer name, phone, ID, purchase date, and dealer stamp. Register the warranty in the OEM's system within 48 hours. Give the customer a physical copy and keep a digital copy.

Also prepare: owner's manual (in the customer's language where possible), service schedule card, and a first-service reminder. For fleet customers (delivery companies, boda boda SACCOs), provide a fleet handover sheet listing every unit's serial numbers.

6. Customer Handover and Basic Training

The handover is a sales and retention event, not a formality. Spend 20â30 minutes with the customer. Cover: (1) how to charge safely â correct voltage, charging location, charging time, and what not to do; (2) how to read the display and battery indicator; (3) daily pre-ride checks (brakes, tyres, lights, throttle response); (4) what to do in a fault â who to call, what not to touch; (5) warranty terms and service intervals; (6) basic troubleshooting (reset procedure, fuse location).

For African riders, emphasize charging safety: many use shared or informal power sources. Explain the risk of overloading sockets, using wrong chargers, and charging in wet conditions. A short, practical demonstration beats a long lecture. Give them a laminated quick-start card in their language.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Torque-check all critical fasteners with a calibrated wrench; record values.
  • â Top off brake fluid, lubricate chain, check for leaks.
  • â Update controller/BMS firmware; calibrate throttle, brake cut-off, speedometer.
  • â Clean and detail using low-pressure water; inspect for cracks and loose parts.
  • â Complete PDI sheet, warranty card, and register warranty within 48 hours.
  • â Confirm frame, motor, battery, and controller serial numbers match documents.
  • â Deliver 20â30 minute customer training on charging, riding, and fault response.
  • â Provide owner's manual, service card, and first-service reminder.

Further Reading

  • U.S. Department of Energy â Electric Vehicle Maintenance
  • NHTSA â Vehicle Safety Standards and Recalls
  • ISO 6469 â Electrically propelled road vehicles: Safety specifications
  • IEC â International Electrotechnical Commission Standards (battery & charging)
  • ILO â Occupational Safety and Health in workshops

Business-first takeaway: The final inspection and handover is your last chance to catch a defect before it becomes a warranty cost, and your best chance to build a customer relationship that generates referrals. In the African e-mobility market, trust is the scarcest resource. A disciplined PDI process is how you earn it â one bike, one rider, one handover at a time.

quiz.q: What is the correct torque for the front axle nut on an EV motorbike?
quiz.explanation: The front axle nut should be tightened to 60 Nm as specified in the lesson.

quiz.q: Which tool must you use to check critical fasteners?
quiz.explanation: A calibrated torque wrench ensures the correct tightness without over- or under-tightening.

quiz.q: What should you do after tightening a critical bolt?
options: A) Mark it with a paint pen
C) Hit it with a hammer
quiz.explanation: Marking with a paint pen shows that the bolt has been checked and torqued.

quiz.q: How often should you recheck torque on critical fasteners after the first ride?
quiz.explanation: Bolts may settle after initial riding, so recheck after 50 km.

quiz.q: What type of brake fluid is commonly used in EV motorbikes?
quiz.explanation: Most EV motorbikes use DOT 3 or DOT 4 brake fluid.

quiz.q: What should you use to top up battery coolant?
options: B) Distilled water and ethylene glycol mix
quiz.explanation: A 50/50 mix of distilled water and ethylene glycol coolant is correct; tap water causes corrosion.

quiz.q: What is the recommended tire pressure for the front tire of an EV motorbike?
quiz.explanation: The front tire should be inflated to 28 psi as stated in the lesson.

quiz.q: How do you clean an EV motorbike's electrical components?
quiz.explanation: Electrical parts like battery and motor should only be wiped with a damp cloth to avoid water damage.

quiz.q: What should you do before applying chain lube?
options: A) Clean the chain with kerosene and brush
quiz.explanation: The chain must be cleaned with kerosene and a brush before lubricating.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of calibrating the throttle?
options: B) To learn zero and full throttle positions
quiz.explanation: Throttle calibration teaches the controller the zero and full positions for smooth operation.

quiz.q: How do you calibrate the battery for the BMS?
options: A) Fully charge, then ride to 20%, then fully charge
quiz.explanation: This cycle helps the BMS learn the true capacity of the battery.

quiz.q: What does error code P0A0F indicate?
quiz.explanation: P0A0F is a common code for motor overheat.

quiz.q: What should you use to wash the bike body?
options: B) Mild car shampoo and water
quiz.explanation: A mild car shampoo and water is safe for painted surfaces; high pressure can damage electronics.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid high-pressure water when washing an EV motorbike?
options: B) It can force water into electrical components
quiz.explanation: High pressure can push water into the battery, controller, and motor, causing damage.

quiz.q: What is the warranty period for the battery on an EV motorbike?
quiz.explanation: The battery warranty is typically 2 years or 20,000 km, whichever comes first.

quiz.q: What documents should be given to the customer at handover?
options: B) Warranty card, owner's manual, and receipt
quiz.explanation: The customer should receive the warranty card, owner's manual, and receipt for proper ownership.

quiz.q: Why should you record serial numbers of the bike, battery, and motor?
quiz.explanation: Serial numbers are needed for warranty claims and to identify the specific components.

quiz.q: What should you do if a customer needs a license plate?
options: B) Help them register with local authorities
C) Tell them to do it themselves
D) Sell them a fake plate
quiz.explanation: Part of good handover is assisting the customer with legal registration.

quiz.q: What is regenerative braking?
options: A) Braking that charges the battery
B) Braking that uses brake fluid
C) Braking that locks the wheel
quiz.explanation: Regenerative braking slows the bike and recovers energy to charge the battery.

quiz.q: When should the customer charge the battery?
options: A) When it is red or low
quiz.explanation: The battery gauge shows green (full), yellow (half), red (charge soon); charge when red or low.

quiz.q: What should you do during a test ride with the customer?
options: A) Let them ride alone immediately
B) You ride first, then they ride in a safe area
quiz.explanation: You should demonstrate first, then let the customer practice in a safe area while you watch.

quiz.q: What is the correct torque for the rear axle nut?
quiz.explanation: The rear axle nut should be tightened to 80 Nm.

quiz.q: Which of these is a daily check for the customer?
quiz.explanation: Daily checks include tires, brakes, lights, and battery level.

quiz.q: What should you use to clean brake calipers?
quiz.explanation: Brake cleaner and a toothbrush effectively remove brake dust without damaging components.

quiz.q: How long should you charge a new EV motorbike battery for a full charge?
quiz.explanation: A full charge typically takes 6-8 hours using the provided charger.

quiz.q: What should you do if a bolt is stripped during torque check?
options: B) Replace with a high-tensile steel bolt
quiz.explanation: A stripped bolt must be replaced with a high-tensile steel bolt of the same size.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of marking bolts with a paint pen?
options: A) To show they are torqued
B) To make them look nice
quiz.explanation: The paint mark indicates that the bolt has been checked and torqued to specification.

quiz.q: What should you do after updating the software?
quiz.explanation: After a software update, you must recalibrate the throttle and battery for proper operation.

quiz.q: What is the first service reminder interval after handover?
quiz.explanation: Send a reminder for the first service after 500 km.

quiz.q: What should you give the customer along with the keys?
quiz.explanation: A small toolkit and all documents (warranty, manual, receipt) should be handed over.
